result.summary: The poet invokes the Muses and announces a war between Mice and Frogs. A mouse, Crumb-snatcher, meets the frog king Puff-jaw, rides on his back across the lake, and is drowned when Puff-jaw dives to escape a water-snake. The Mice, told of the death, gather to hear Bread-nibbler.

scenes.title: Invocation to the Muses
scenes.summary: The poet asks the Muses to help him tell of the war of Mice and Frogs.

scenes.title: Puff-jaw meets Crumb-snatcher
scenes.summary: A thirsty mouse drinks at the lake and is questioned by the frog king. Each tells his lineage, and Crumb-snatcher explains his foods and fears.
scenes.stakes: Crumb-snatcher risks danger by trusting a stranger from a different world.

scenes.title: The ride across the lake
scenes.summary: Puff-jaw boasts of the frogs' double life and offers a ride. The mouse grows terrified as the waves wash over him.
scenes.stakes: Crumb-snatcher's life, as he is carried over deep water.

scenes.title: The water-snake and the drowning
scenes.summary: A water-snake appears and Puff-jaw dives, abandoning the mouse. Crumb-snatcher curses him and drowns.

scenes.title: The Mice assemble
scenes.summary: Lick-platter sees the death and tells the Mice, who gather at dawn at Bread-nibbler's house. Bread-nibbler rises to speak.
scenes.stakes: The Mice face the choice of war to avenge a killing.

alias_notes.explanation: A title for Jove (Zeus), son of Chronos, though the translation does not name him.

notable_quotes.reason: Mock-heroic comparison of the frog's back to the bull carrying Europa.
The dying mouse's curse that sets up the war.

analysis.text: The poem parodies epic: an invocation, genealogies and heroic boasts are applied to tiny animals, making their quarrel comic.
Betrayal and misplaced trust trigger the war, as a small accident grows into a conflict.

legacy.text: The Battle of Frogs and Mice was traditionally attributed to Homer and was widely read and imitated as a model of mock-epic, influencing later works such as Pope's The Rape of the Lock.

fun_facts.text: The poem was long credited to Homer, but scholars generally date it much later, probably Hellenistic or even Roman times.

language_notes.text: Helicon is a mountain in Boeotia sacred to the Muses; poets traditionally invoke them from there.
"Tablets upon my knee" means writing tablets held on the lap; the poet presents his poem as freshly composed in writing.
The Giants were earth-born beings who battled the gods; the mock-epic compares the mice's small war to this great mythic conflict.
"Fain" means gladly or willingly; "lay" elsewhere means a song or poem.
"Pond-larker" is the translator's playful compound for a frog, in the manner of epic epithets.
Eridanus is a legendary river, often associated with the Po; naming it lends the frog's pedigree mock grandeur.
A quern is a hand mill for grain, so "Quern-licker" suits a mouse's name.
"Cates" are delicacies or choice foods; "quern" earlier names a hand mill for grinding grain.
"Belly-matters" means food and eating; Puff-jaw teases the Mouse for boasting only of his meals.
"'Tis" is a contraction of "it is"; "lest" means "for fear that."
Refers to the myth in which Jove, as a bull, carried Europa across the sea to Crete.
"Castaway" here means one cast off or abandoned, comparing the Mouse to something thrown from a rock.
"Heaven has an avenging eye" means the gods watch wrongdoing and see that it is punished.
"Heralds" were official messengers who summoned assemblies and announced public business.

context_notes.text: Ferrets were kept in ancient households to hunt mice, so the mouse's fear of one is natural.
Puff-jaw is the frog king; the poem gives animals comic compound names in imitation of epic heroes.
The foods listed are human household fare, stressing how mice live among men, unlike water-dwelling frogs.
The Son of Chronos is Jove (the Greek Zeus), king of the gods, here credited with making frogs amphibious.
The water-snake is a natural enemy of frogs, which explains Puff-jaw's instant panic.

literary_notes.text: Opening with a call to the Muses follows the epic convention, here applied to a comic subject.
Comparing mice and frogs to the Giants' war inflates a trivial conflict into heroic grandeur, producing humour.
The frog's pompous royal self-introduction in epic style is comic, given that he rules a pond.
Crumb-snatcher boasts of boldness yet describes only nibbling a sleeper's toe, revealing a comically small kind of bravery.
His list of fears hints that danger and death will shape the coming war.
The tail is called a steering oar, giving the Mouse's desperate effort the dignity of a ship's seamanship.
The Mouse compares his shabby ride to a grand myth, a mock-heroic touch that makes his plight comic.
The host who promised a joyful ride abandons his guest, and the frog's boast of safety in two elements saves only himself.
The dying Mouse addresses the absent Puff-jaw directly, voicing a curse that sets up the coming war.
